claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by a narrow kinetic window during nucleation.
Successful alloy formation requires a balance between precursor-reduction rates and atomic-interdiffusion rates.
Reduction that is sufficiently slow permits enough intermixing to form a homogeneous alloy.
Excessively rapid reduction kinetically traps atoms and produces phase segregation and uncontrolled morphology.
Moderating the thermal profile can moderate the reduction rate.
A moderated thermal profile permits sufficient atomic interdiffusion during nucleation.
Changing the rate of temperature increase changes the reduction kinetics while the precursor mixture and environment remain fixed.
Atomic-level mixing occurs during nucleation and early particle growth.
A slower, appropriately timed reduction enhances interdiffusion among metal atoms during nucleation.
Enhanced interdiffusion during nucleation leads to a uniform alloy structure.
Rapid reduction freezes atoms into place before they can interdiffuse.
Premature kinetic trapping causes elemental segregation, distinct phases, or uncontrolled morphology.
A slower thermal profile will produce nanoparticles with a significantly more homogeneous elemental distribution than a rapid-reduction baseline.
The rapid-reduction baseline routinely produces phase-separated domains and heterogeneous compositions.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems whose reduction potentials and atomic diffusion coefficients are sufficiently similar to be modulated by the thermal profile.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when reduction kinetics are extremely disparate.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when diffusion barriers are too high for meaningful intermixing during nucleation.
